title: Annual Diabetes Patient Education
subtitle: For staff at Pennsylvania personal care homes who administer insulin or provide diabetes-related care. 55 Pa. Code 2600.190(b) and (c).

title: Sugar, the key, and the two types
points: Sugar is fuel; it rides in the blood
It needs a key to get into cells
Insulin is the key
Type 1: the key is not made at all
Type 2: the lock has gotten stiff

eyebrow: Two different things that look alike
quote: Carrying out an order and deciding a dose are not the same job, and only one of them is yours.
attribution: Adding a couple of units because the number looks high is a prescriber's decision made by someone who is not the prescriber.

title: Getting a reading you can trust
points: Dry the finger completely first
Side of the fingertip, not the pad
Let the drop come; do not squeeze
One lancet, one person, then sharps
Write the number down right then

eyebrow: When the meter and the person disagree
quote: Treat the resident in front of you, according to the resident's own order.
attribution: A meter is a tool. Someone sweating and confused is the actual situation, whatever the screen says.

eyebrow: First the alarm, then the brain
title: What low blood sugar looks like
points: Sweating, cool and clammy skin
Shaking, racing heart, sudden hunger
Anxiety with nothing attached to it
Confusion, slurred or rambling speech
Anger or tears from someone calm

quote: Nothing goes in the mouth. Not juice, not gel, not a tablet in the cheek.
attribution: Someone who cannot protect their airway will aspirate it, and now they have a low blood sugar and a lung full of juice.

title: What high blood sugar looks like
points: Urinating more, up through the night
Thirsty, dry mouth, drinking constantly
Weak, tired, blurred vision
Then confused, drowsy, hard to wake
Often an infection nobody has found

quote: Recognize that it is serious. Do not decide which one it is.
attribution: Ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar state are both life-threatening and neither is yours to diagnose. Vomiting, odd breathing, or hard to rouse is an emergency now.

title: Five shapes of insulin
points: Rapid-acting: around a meal
Short-acting: also mealtime, slower
Intermediate: broad peak mid-run
Long-acting: background, roughly daily
Premixed: two of those, fixed ratio

quote: Same amount of liquid. Several times as many units in it.
attribution: A device built for one concentration does not measure another. Read the concentration against the order every time, and never convert it yourself.

title: Keeping insulin worth giving
points: Unopened: refrigerated, off the back wall
In use: the maker's period, not a habit
Date it when you open it
Frozen once is finished forever
Clumps, crystals, unreadable label: stop

title: Reading the order and the MAR
What a complete order contains
points: The right resident
The insulin, full name and suffix
The concentration
The dose, in units, an actual number
The route and the time

quote: You are not refusing to work. You are refusing to guess.
attribution: A scale that stops at 299 has no instruction for 312. Do not extend it. Stop, get it clarified, and report the number.

eyebrow: The lines are not the same
title: Before you draw anything
points: Smallest syringe that holds the dose
Work out what one line means
On some 100-unit syringes, one line is 2
Clear the bubbles, re-pull to the mark
Read it at eye level, never from above

title: Pens differ from each other
points: New needle for every injection
Prime it the way that maker says
Dial it, then read the dose window
Hold the needle in for their count
No name on it: report, do not relabel

eyebrow: Why rotation is not a formality
title: Sites and skin
points: Abdomen, outer arms, thighs, buttocks
Move a finger's width from the last one
Same spot repeatedly thickens the tissue
Thick tissue absorbs unpredictably
Not into bruised, broken or lumpy skin

eyebrow: A blank space is not a record
quote: A refusal, a held dose and an omitted dose are all real events with real documentation.
attribution: Document at the point of care, with the reason and who you told. Never as though it happened, never left empty.

eyebrow: In this order, and the order is the point
title: What to do about an error
points: Stop. Do not finish the dose
Protect the resident, before paperwork
Report it through your process now
Get clinical or emergency help
A near miss gets reported too

eyebrow: Two things that are never the response
quote: You do not fix a dose yourself, and you do not wait to see whether anything happens.
attribution: The whole point of reporting fast is that somebody can still act. Insulin given an hour ago is still working.

eyebrow: Often two of them at once
title: Which one are you in
points: Proceed: the order is complete
Stop and clarify: something is missing
Notify: outside their parameters
Emergency: danger right now
You are the person who notices
